questions.questionText: What happens when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to iron fillings? Tick the correct answer.

**Solution:**

\]

questions.questionText: What is a balanced chemical equation? Why should chemical equations be balanced?
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

A balanced chemical equation is a chemical equation in which the number of atoms of each element on the reactant side is equal to the number of atoms of the same element on the product side.

For example, the burning of magnesium in oxygen is represented as

\[
2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}
\]

Here, the number of magnesium atoms and oxygen atoms is the same on both sides of the arrow, so the equation is balanced.

Chemical equations must be balanced because of the law of conservation of mass. According to this law, mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Since atoms are neither gained nor lost during a reaction, the total mass of the reactants must equal the total mass of the products. An unbalanced equation would show a change in the number of atoms, which is not possible in a chemical reaction.

Therefore, balancing a chemical equation makes it consistent with the law of conservation of mass and correctly represents the actual quantities of reactants and products involved in the reaction.

questions.questionText:
Translate the following statements into chemical equations and then balance them.
(a) Hydrogen gas combines with nitrogen to form ammonia.
(b) Hydrogen sulphide gas burns in air to give water and sulphur dioxide.
(c) Barium chloride reacts with aluminium sulphate to give aluminium chloride and a precipitate of barium sulphate.
(d) Potassium metal reacts with water to give potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

**(a) Hydrogen gas combines with nitrogen to form ammonia.**

Word equation:
\[
\text{Hydrogen} + \text{Nitrogen} \longrightarrow \text{Ammonia}
\]

Chemical equation (unbalanced):
\[
\text{H}_2 + \text{N}_2 \longrightarrow \text{NH}_3
\]

Balancing the nitrogen atoms by placing a coefficient of \(2\) before \(\text{NH}_3\), and then balancing the hydrogen atoms by placing a coefficient of \(3\) before \(\text{H}_2\):
\[
3\text{H}_2 + \text{N}_2 \longrightarrow 2\text{NH}_3
\]

---

**(b) Hydrogen sulphide gas burns in air to give water and sulphur dioxide.**

Word equation:
\[
\text{Hydrogen sulphide} + \text{Oxygen} \longrightarrow \text{Water} + \text{Sulphur dioxide}
\]

Chemical equation (unbalanced):
\[
\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \longrightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{SO}_2
\]

Balancing the hydrogen and sulphur atoms first, and then adjusting the oxygen atoms, we obtain:
\[
2\text{H}_2\text{S} + 3\text{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{SO}_2
\]

---

**(c) Barium chloride reacts with aluminium sulphate to give aluminium chloride and a precipitate of barium sulphate.**

Word equation:
\[
\text{Barium chloride} + \text{Aluminium sulphate} \longrightarrow \text{Aluminium chloride} + \text{Barium sulphate}
\]

Chemical equation (unbalanced):
\[
\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 \longrightarrow \text{AlCl}_3 + \text{BaSO}_4
\]

Balancing the sulphate groups and chloride ions by placing appropriate coefficients gives:
\[
3\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 \longrightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{BaSO}_4
\]

---

**(d) Potassium metal reacts with water to give potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.**

Word equation:
\[
\text{Potassium} + \text{Water} \longrightarrow \text{Potassium hydroxide} + \text{Hydrogen}
\]

Chemical equation (unbalanced):
\[
\text{K} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{KOH} + \text{H}_2
\]

Balancing the hydrogen and oxygen atoms by adjusting the coefficients of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), \(\text{KOH}\), and \(\text{K}\):
\[
2\text{K} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2\text{KOH} + \text{H}_2
\]

Write the balanced chemical equations for the following reactions.
(a) Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide → Calcium carbonate + Water
(b) Zinc + Silver nitrate → Zinc nitrate + Silver
(c) Aluminium + Copper chloride → Aluminium chloride + Copper
(d) Barium chloride + Potassium sulphate → Barium sulphate + Potassium chloride
questions.solutionText:
**Solution:**

The balanced chemical equations for the given reactions are:

**(a)** Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide \(\rightarrow\) Calcium carbonate + Water
\[
\text{Ca(OH)}_2\text{ (aq)} + \text{CO}_2\text{ (g)} \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3\text{ (s)} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\text{ (l)}
\]

**(b)** Zinc + Silver nitrate \(\rightarrow\) Zinc nitrate + Silver
\[
\text{Zn}\text{ (s)} + 2\text{AgNO}_3\text{ (aq)} \rightarrow \text{Zn(NO}_3)_2\text{ (aq)} + 2\text{Ag}\text{ (s)}
\]

**(c)** Aluminium + Copper chloride \(\rightarrow\) Aluminium chloride + Copper
\[
2\text{Al}\text{ (s)} + 3\text{CuCl}_2\text{ (aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3\text{ (aq)} + 3\text{Cu}\text{ (s)}
\]

**(d)** Barium chloride + Potassium sulphate \(\rightarrow\) Barium sulphate + Potassium chloride
\[
\text{BaCl}_2\text{ (aq)} + \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4\text{ (aq)} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4\text{ (s)} + 2\text{KCl}\text{ (aq)}
\]

questions.questionText:
Write the balanced chemical equation for the following and identify the type of reaction in each case.
(a) Potassium bromide(aq) + Barium iodide(aq) → Potassium iodide(aq) + Barium bromide(s)
(b) Zinc carbonate(s) → Zinc oxide(s) + Carbon dioxide(g)
(c) Hydrogen(g) + Chlorine(g) → Hydrogen chloride(g)
(d) Magnesium(s) + Hydrochloric acid(aq) → Magnesium chloride(aq) + Hydrogen(g)
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

**(a)** Potassium bromide reacts with barium iodide to form potassium iodide and barium bromide.

\[
2\text{KBr}(aq) + \text{BaI}_2(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{KI}(aq) + \text{BaBr}_2(s)
\]

Here, the ions of the two reactants exchange partners to form two new compounds, and barium bromide is obtained as a precipitate. Hence, it is a **double displacement reaction** (precipitation reaction).

**(b)** Zinc carbonate on heating decomposes to give zinc oxide and carbon dioxide.

\[
\text{ZnCO}_3(s) \rightarrow \text{ZnO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)
\]

A single compound breaks down into two simpler substances. Hence, it is a **decomposition reaction** (thermal decomposition).

**(c)** Hydrogen combines with chlorine to form hydrogen chloride.

\[
\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}(g)
\]

Two substances combine to form a single new substance. Hence, it is a **combination reaction**.

**(d)** Magnesium displaces hydrogen from hydrochloric acid.

\[
\text{Mg}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)
\]

A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. Hence, it is a **displacement reaction**.

questions.questionText: What does one mean by exothermic and endothermic reactions? Give examples.
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

An **exothermic reaction** is a chemical reaction in which heat is released along with the formation of products. In such reactions, the temperature of the reaction mixture rises.

Example: Burning of natural gas (methane):

\[
\text{CH}_4 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{heat}
\]

Another example is respiration, which also releases energy.

An **endothermic reaction** is a chemical reaction in which heat is absorbed. In such reactions, the temperature of the reaction mixture falls.

Example: Decomposition of calcium carbonate on heating:

\[
\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{heat} \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2
\]

Another example is the decomposition of lead(II) nitrate on heating:

\[
2\text{Pb(NO}_3\text{)}_2(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{PbO}(s) + 4\text{NO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)
\]

In this reaction, lead(II) nitrate absorbs heat and decomposes into lead(II) oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and oxygen. Since heat is absorbed, it is an endothermic reaction.

questions.questionText: Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction? Explain.
questions.solutionText:
Respiration is considered an exothermic reaction because it releases energy.

During respiration, glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen to form carbon dioxide, water, and energy.

\[
C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + \text{Energy}
\]

The energy stored in glucose is released during this oxidation process. Some of this energy is used by the body for its activities, and the rest is released as heat. Since the overall reaction releases energy, respiration is an exothermic reaction.

questions.questionText: Why are decomposition reactions called the opposite of combination reactions? Write equations for these reactions.
questions.solutionText:
Decomposition reactions are called the opposite of combination reactions because in a combination reaction two or more reactants combine to form a single product, whereas in a decomposition reaction a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. Thus, the products of a combination reaction can act as the reactants of a decomposition reaction, and vice versa.

For example:

**Combination reaction:**
\[
\mathrm{CaO(s)+CO_2(g)\rightarrow CaCO_3(s)}
\]

**Decomposition reaction:**
\[
\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)\xrightarrow{\Delta} CaO(s)+CO_2(g)}
\]

Therefore, decomposition reactions are the reverse of combination reactions.

questions.questionText: Write one equation each for decomposition reactions where energy is supplied in the form of heat, light or electricity.
questions.solutionText:
The equation for each of the decomposition reactions with heat, light or electricity are as follows: 

**1. By heat (thermal decomposition):**

\[
{CaCO3(s) ->[\Delta] CaO(s) + CO2(g)}
\]

**2. By light (photochemical decomposition):**

\[
{2AgCl(s) ->[\text{sunlight}] 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)}
\]

**3. By electricity (electrolytic decomposition):**

\[
{2H2O(l) ->[\text{electricity}] 2H2(g) + O2(g)}
\]

These are decomposition reactions because in each case a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between displacement and double displacement reactions? Write equations for these reactions.
questions.solutionText:
**Solution:**

The difference between displacement and double displacement reactions lies in how the atoms or ions exchange between reactants.

*   **Displacement Reaction:** A chemical reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its aqueous salt solution. These reactions are generally single replacement reactions of the form \(A + BC \rightarrow AC + B\).
*   **Double Displacement Reaction:** A chemical reaction in which two different atoms or groups of atoms (ions) are exchanged between two reactants to form two new compounds. These reactions generally take the form \(AB + CD \rightarrow AD + CB\) and often result in the formation of a precipitate.

### Equations for Reactions

**1. Displacement Reaction**
When an iron nail is dipped in a copper sulfate solution, iron displaces copper from the copper sulfate solution to form ferrous sulfate and copper metal.

\[
\text{Fe(s)} + \text{CuSO}_4(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(\text{aq}) + \text{Cu(s)}
\]

**2. Double Displacement Reaction**
When an aqueous solution of sodium sulfate is mixed with an aqueous solution of barium chloride, a white precipitate of barium sulfate is formed along with sodium chloride.

\[
\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{aq}) + \text{BaCl}_2(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(\text{s}) \downarrow + 2\text{NaCl}(\text{aq})
\]

questions.questionText: In the refining of silver, the recovery of silver from silver nitrate solution involved displacement by copper metal. Write down the reaction involved.
questions.solutionText:
**Solution:**

Copper is more reactive than silver, so it displaces silver from silver nitrate solution.

\[
{Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) -> Cu(NO3)2(aq) + 2Ag(s)}
\]

In ionic form:

\[
{Cu(s) + 2Ag+(aq) -> Cu^2+(aq) + 2Ag(s)}
\]

Therefore, the reaction involved is the displacement of silver by copper from silver nitrate solution.

questions.questionText: What do you mean by a precipitation reaction? Explain by giving examples.
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

**Definition**

A precipitation reaction is a chemical reaction in which two soluble salts in aqueous solution react to form an insoluble solid, called a precipitate. It is a type of double displacement reaction.

**Examples**

1. When silver nitrate solution is mixed with sodium chloride solution, a white precipitate of silver chloride is formed.

\[
\text{AgNO}_3(aq) + \text{NaCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)\downarrow + \text{NaNO}_3(aq)
\]

Here, silver chloride is insoluble in water and separates out as a white precipitate.

2. When barium chloride solution is mixed with sodium sulphate solution, a white precipitate of barium sulphate is formed.

\[
\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)\downarrow + 2\text{NaCl}(aq)
\]

Here, barium sulphate is insoluble and appears as a white precipitate.

Therefore, a precipitation reaction involves the formation of an insoluble solid (precipitate) by the exchange of ions between two soluble salts in aqueous solution.

questions.questionText:
Explain the following in terms of gain or loss of oxygen with two examples each.
(a) Oxidation
(b) Reduction
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

**(a) Oxidation:** Oxidation is a chemical change in which a substance gains oxygen.

Examples:

- When copper is heated in air, it gains oxygen to form copper(II) oxide.
\[
2\text{Cu} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CuO}
\]
Here, copper is oxidised.

- When magnesium burns in air, it gains oxygen to form magnesium oxide.
\[
2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}
\]
Here, magnesium is oxidised.

**(b) Reduction:** Reduction is a chemical change in which a substance loses oxygen.

Examples:

- When copper(II) oxide is heated with hydrogen, it loses oxygen to form copper.
\[
\text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O}
\]
Here, copper(II) oxide is reduced to copper.

- When zinc oxide is heated with carbon, it loses oxygen to form zinc.
\[
\text{ZnO} + \text{C} \rightarrow \text{Zn} + \text{CO}
\]
Here, zinc oxide is reduced to zinc.

Therefore, oxidation involves gain of oxygen, while reduction involves loss of oxygen.

questions.questionText: A shiny brown coloured element 'X' on heating in air becomes black in colour. Name the element 'X' and the black coloured compound formed.
questions.solutionText:
The shiny brown coloured element is copper.

\[
\text{X} = \text{Copper (Cu)}
\]

On heating copper in air, it reacts with oxygen to form black copper(II) oxide.

\[
2\text{Cu} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CuO}
\]

Therefore, the element is copper, and the black coloured compound formed is copper(II) oxide \((\text{CuO})\).

questions.questionText: Why do we apply paint on iron articles?
questions.solutionText:
Paint is applied on iron articles to protect them from rusting.

Iron rusts when it comes in contact with air and moisture. A layer of paint forms a protective coating on the surface of the iron article and prevents direct contact with air and moisture. Thus, painting helps in preventing corrosion of iron.

questions.questionText: Oil and fat containing food items are flushed with nitrogen. Why?
questions.solutionText:
Oil and fat containing food items undergo oxidation when exposed to oxygen, which makes them rancid and gives them an unpleasant smell and taste.

Nitrogen is chemically inert and does not react with oils and fats. When such food items are flushed with nitrogen, oxygen is displaced from the packet, preventing oxidation.

Therefore, oil and fat containing food items are flushed with nitrogen to prevent rancidity and to keep them fresh for a longer time.

questions.questionText:
Explain the following terms with one example each.
(a) Corrosion
(b) Rancidity
questions.solutionText:
**20. (a) Corrosion**

Corrosion is the process in which a metal is gradually eaten away by the action of air, moisture, or chemicals such as acids on its surface. The metal gets covered with a layer of its oxide, hydroxide, or carbonate, and loses its shine and strength.

**Example:** When iron is left exposed to moist air, it gets coated with a reddish-brown flaky layer of hydrated iron(III) oxide, commonly called rust. This is known as the rusting of iron.

\[
4\text{Fe} + 3\text{O}_2 + x\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}
\]

Other examples include the green coating on copper and the black coating on silver.

**(b) Rancidity**

Rancidity is the process in which fats and oils present in food materials get oxidised on exposure to air, moisture, or light, causing an unpleasant change in their smell and taste. Such food is said to have become rancid and is unfit for eating.

**Example:** Butter kept outside for a long time turns rancid. The fats present in it are oxidised by atmospheric oxygen, and the butter develops a foul smell and a sour taste.

Rancidity can be delayed by adding antioxidants, by packing food in airtight containers, or by storing it in a refrigerator.

questions.questionText:
Which of the statements about the reaction below are incorrect?
2PbO(s) + C(s) → 2Pb(s) + CO2(g)
(a) Lead is getting reduced.
(b) Carbon dioxide is getting oxidised.
(c) Carbon is getting oxidised.
(d) Lead oxide is getting reduced.
questions.solutionText:
**Solution:**

**Given:**
The chemical reaction:
\[
2\text{PbO(s)} + \text{C(s)} \rightarrow 2\text{Pb(s)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}
\]

**Analysis of the Reaction:**
- **Reduction** is defined as the addition of hydrogen or removal of oxygen, or gain of electrons. In this reaction, lead(II) oxide (\(\text{PbO}\)) loses oxygen to form lead (\(\text{Pb}\)). Therefore, **Lead oxide (\(\text{PbO}\)) is getting reduced**. Consequently, statement (d) is correct, while statement (a) ("Lead is getting reduced") is incorrect because the element lead itself is the product formed after reduction, not the substance undergoing reduction.
- **Oxidation** is defined as the addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen, or loss of electrons. In this reaction, carbon (\(\text{C}\)) gains oxygen to form carbon dioxide (\(\text{CO}_2\)). Therefore, **Carbon (\(\text{C}\)) is getting oxidised**. Consequently, statement (c) is correct, while statement (b) ("Carbon dioxide is getting oxidised") is incorrect because carbon dioxide is the product of oxidation, not the substance getting oxidised.

Thus, the incorrect statements among the given choices are (a) and (b).

Therefore, the correct option is **(A)**.

questions.questionText: Why should a magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning in air?
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

Magnesium is a reactive metal. On exposure to air, it reacts with atmospheric oxygen to form a thin, stable layer of magnesium oxide on its surface:

\[
2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}
\]

This oxide layer is chemically inert and coats the ribbon, preventing the underlying magnesium from coming into direct contact with oxygen. As a result, the ribbon does not burn readily or may burn with a dull flame.

Rubbing the ribbon with sandpaper removes this oxide layer and exposes the fresh, shiny surface of the metal. The exposed magnesium then reacts easily with oxygen and burns in air with a dazzling white flame.

Therefore, a magnesium ribbon is cleaned before burning to remove the layer of magnesium oxide so that the fresh metal surface is exposed for combustion.

questions.questionText:
Write the balanced equation for the following chemical reactions.
(i) Hydrogen + Chlorine → Hydrogen chloride
(ii) Barium chloride + Aluminium sulphate → Barium sulphate + Aluminium chloride
(iii) Sodium + Water → Sodium hydroxide + Hydrogen
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

**(i) Hydrogen + Chlorine → Hydrogen chloride**

Word equation:

\[
\text{Hydrogen} + \text{Chlorine} \rightarrow \text{Hydrogen chloride}
\]

Balanced chemical equation:

\[
\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}
\]

**(ii) Barium chloride + Aluminium sulphate → Barium sulphate + Aluminium chloride**

Word equation:

\[
\text{Barium chloride} + \text{Aluminium sulphate} \rightarrow \text{Barium sulphate} + \text{Aluminium chloride}
\]

Balanced chemical equation:

\[
3\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 \rightarrow 3\text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{AlCl}_3
\]

**(iii) Sodium + Water → Sodium hydroxide + Hydrogen**

Word equation:

\[
\text{Sodium} + \text{Water} \rightarrow \text{Sodium hydroxide} + \text{Hydrogen}
\]

Balanced chemical equation:

\[
2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2
\]

Therefore, the balanced chemical equations are:

\[
\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}
\]

\[
3\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 \rightarrow 3\text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{AlCl}_3
\]

\[
2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2
\]

questions.questionText:
Write a balanced chemical equation with state symbols for the following reactions.
(i) Solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate in water react to give insoluble barium sulphate and the solution of sodium chloride.
(ii) Sodium hydroxide solution (in water) reacts with hydrochloric acid solution (in water) to produce sodium chloride solution and water.
questions.solutionText:
(i) Aqueous barium chloride reacts with aqueous sodium sulphate to form a precipitate of barium sulphate and aqueous sodium chloride:

\[
\mathrm{BaCl_2(aq) + Na_2SO_4(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}
\]

(ii) Aqueous sodium hydroxide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to form aqueous sodium chloride and water:

\[
\mathrm{NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)}
\]

Therefore, the required balanced chemical equations with state symbols are:

\[
\boxed{\mathrm{BaCl_2(aq) + Na_2SO_4(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}}
\]

\[
\boxed{\mathrm{NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)}}
\]

questions.questionText:
A solution of a substance 'X' is used for whitewashing.
(i) Name the substance 'X' and write its formula.
(ii) Write the reaction of the substance 'X' named in (i) above with water.
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

(i) The substance \(X\) is **calcium oxide**, commonly called **quick lime**.  
Its chemical formula is:

\[
\text{CaO}
\]

(ii) Calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide, which is used for whitewashing:

\[
\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{heat}
\]

Therefore, the substance \(X\) is calcium oxide, \(\text{CaO}\), and it reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide, \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\).

questions.questionText: Why is the amount of gas collected in one of the test tubes in Activity 1.7 double of the amount collected in the other? Name this gas.
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

In Activity 1.7, electric current is passed through acidified water, which decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen:

\[
2\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{electric current}} 2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2
\]

A water molecule contains two atoms of hydrogen and one atom of oxygen, that is, hydrogen and oxygen are present in the ratio \(2:1\) by volume. Since the composition of water is fixed, the gases are always liberated in this same ratio during electrolysis.

Consequently, the test tube connected to the cathode (negative electrode) collects twice the volume of gas collected in the test tube connected to the anode. The gas collected in larger amount is **hydrogen**, while the gas collected in the smaller amount is oxygen.

Therefore, the gas collected in double the amount is **hydrogen**.

questions.questionText: Why does the colour of copper sulphate solution change when an iron nail is dipped in it?
questions.solutionText:
When an iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution, a displacement reaction takes place because iron is more reactive than copper.

\[
\text{Fe}(s)+\text{CuSO}_4(aq)\rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq)+\text{Cu}(s)
\]

Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution. The blue colour of copper sulphate solution is due to \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) ions. As these copper ions are displaced and converted into copper metal, their concentration in the solution decreases. Therefore, the blue colour fades and the solution becomes light green due to the formation of ferrous sulphate.

A reddish-brown coating of copper is also deposited on the iron nail.

Thus, the colour change occurs because copper sulphate is converted into ferrous sulphate, while copper metal is deposited on the iron nail.

questions.questionText: Give an example of a double displacement reaction other than the one given in Activity 1.10.
questions.solutionText:
When lead(II) nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution, a yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide is formed.

\[
\mathrm{Pb(NO_3)_2(aq) + 2KI(aq) \rightarrow PbI_2(s) + 2KNO_3(aq)}
\]

In this reaction, the ions of the two reactants exchange partners, so it is a double displacement reaction.

questions.questionText:
Identify the substances that are oxidised and the substances that are reduced in the following reactions.
(i) 4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s)
(ii) CuO(s) + H2(g) → Cu(s) + H2O(l)
questions.solutionText:
**Solution**

(i) In the reaction

\[
4\mathrm{Na(s)}+\mathrm{O_2(g)}\rightarrow 2\mathrm{Na_2O(s)}
\]

sodium changes from oxidation state \(0\) in \(\mathrm{Na}\) to \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\). Hence, sodium is oxidised.

Oxygen changes from oxidation state \(0\) in \(\mathrm{O_2}\) to \(-2\) in \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\). Hence, oxygen is reduced.

Therefore, \(\mathrm{Na}\) is oxidised and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is reduced.

(ii) In the reaction

\[
\mathrm{CuO(s)}+\mathrm{H_2(g)}\rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}+\mathrm{H_2O(l)}
\]

copper changes from oxidation state \(+2\) in \(\mathrm{CuO}\) to \(0\) in \(\mathrm{Cu}\). Hence, \(\mathrm{CuO}\) is reduced.

Hydrogen changes from oxidation state \(0\) in \(\mathrm{H_2}\) to \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{H_2O}\). Hence, \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is oxidised.

Therefore, \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is oxidised and \(\mathrm{CuO}\) is reduced.
